#### Why these are two views rather than two kinds of data

**A stream is motion.** Each of this book's 9 records is a *change*: id 0 adds 5 to key "a", and so on. To answer "what is key `a` now?" you have to read all of them and add up. A stream answers **what happened**.

**A table is state.** Fold those records per key and you get 2 rows: "a" = 24, "b" = 21. One lookup, no arithmetic. A table answers **what is true now**.

**They are the same data.** Both views total **45** — the stream over 9 records, the table over 2 rows. That equality is the duality in its most checkable form: neither view invented or lost anything, they are arranged for different questions.

What each gives up is precise. The table has forgotten the **order** and every **intermediate value** — ask it "was key `a` ever 8?" and it cannot answer, though the stream can. The stream has given up cheap lookups: every current value is a fold.

**And that is why the industry split the way it did.** A relational database is table-centric: it stores the 2 rows and derives history only if someone built an audit table. An event log is stream-centric: it stores the 9 records and derives the rows on read. A stream processor sits between them, consuming the stream and maintaining the table.

So "database or event log?" is usually the wrong question. The real one is **which view is the source and which is derived** — and neither is primary by nature. The stream earns that role only because the derivation is cheap in one direction.

#### When to reach for each view, and what the choice commits you to

**Query the table for "what is true now"**, which is almost all production traffic. It is a lookup against 2 rows rather than a fold over 9 records, and the gap widens as history accumulates.

**Query the stream for anything about order or history** — "what happened", "what was it at time T", "was it ever X". These are unanswerable from the table at any cost, because the information is gone rather than merely slow to reach.

**Choose which view is the source deliberately, and only once.** A derived view can lag, which is visible and bounded. Two independently written stores **drift**, which is unbounded and silent, and "keep them in sync" is not a design — a derivation is.

**What this does not settle:** whether the derivation actually runs both ways. The next concept shows that aggregating a changelog always recovers the table, and recovers the original events only when the aggregate is invertible — so "the two directions are inverses" turns out to be a property of the aggregate rather than of the duality.

A stream answers "what happened". Each of the 9 rows is a change, so the current value of anything is a computation rather than a lookup. In exchange you get something a table throws away: the order, and every value the system ever held.

<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the table: what is true now</summary>

A table answers "what is true now" in a lookup rather than a fold: 9 records collapse to 2 rows. The cost is in the note — the table has forgotten the order and every intermediate value, so a question about history is unanswerable from it even though no information was deliberately discarded.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — and they are the same data, folded differently</summary>

Both totals are 45, which is the duality in its most checkable form: the two views contain the same information, arranged for different questions. The second note is the design consequence — neither is inherently the source of truth, and the stream earns that role because the derivation only runs one way cheaply.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — so databases and event logs each picked a side</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-faces/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: so databases and event logs each picked a side" width="1040">

Reading the industry split this way makes the architectural choice concrete. A database stores 2 rows and can give you history only if someone added an audit table; a log stores 9 records and makes every lookup a fold. The useful question is never which technology — it is which of the two views you treat as truth.
